name: Subnetting
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Find the subnet, broadcast, and host range for any address and mask in seconds, size subnets, and design VLSM plans.

lesson.intro: Subnetting is the single most practiced skill on the CCNA: it hides inside questions about routing tables, ACLs, OSPF, DHCP pools, and troubleshooting. This lesson gives you a fast decimal method (the magic number), the binary method it is built on, and then the design side: picking masks, building VLSM plans, sizing point-to-point links, and summarizing routes, with the traps that cost people points.
objectives: Find the subnet ID, broadcast address, and usable host range for any address and prefix, in any octet
Calculate hosts per subnet (2^h - 2) and number of subnets (2^s) and choose a mask that meets a requirement
Design a VLSM plan from largest to smallest subnet and spot overlapping subnets
Choose /30 or /31 for point-to-point links and summarize contiguous subnets into one route
Avoid the classic traps: subnet zero, off-by-one host counts, and working in the wrong octet

sections.title: Why subnet, and the two formulas
sections.body:
A company owns 172.16.0.0/16: 65,534 host addresses in one block. It has 150 sites, each with several VLANs, plus WAN links between them. Every LAN, VLAN, and router-to-router link needs its own subnet, because a router interface sits in exactly one subnet and broadcasts must stay contained. **Subnetting** carves the big block into many smaller ones.

You do it by borrowing bits. The original network keeps its prefix bits, and some of its host bits become **subnet bits**. The host bits that remain number the hosts inside each subnet. Borrowing 8 bits from 172.16.0.0/16 gives a /24 mask: 16 network bits, 8 subnet bits, 8 host bits.

Two formulas answer most sizing questions:

- **Number of subnets = 2^s**, where s is the number of borrowed bits (the new prefix minus the original prefix).
- **Usable hosts per subnet = 2^h - 2**, where h is the number of host bits left (32 minus the prefix).

So 172.16.0.0/16 cut into /22s has s = 6, giving 64 subnets, and h = 10, giving 1,022 hosts in each.

Hosts lose 2 because in every subnet the all-zeros host value is the subnet ID and the all-ones value is the broadcast. Subnets lose nothing. Long ago, engineers avoided the first subnet (the **zero subnet**, which has the same number as the original network, like 172.16.0.0/24) and the last one (the all-ones or broadcast subnet), and old books used 2^s - 2. IOS has allowed both by default for years (`ip subnet-zero` is the default), and the current CCNA exam treats them as usable unless a question explicitly says otherwise.

Memorize the powers of 2 up to 2^12. You will use them in almost every question.
sections.tip: Hosts: subtract 2. Subnets: do not. Say it until it is automatic.
sections.pitfall: Using 2^s - 2 for the number of subnets. That rule dates from before subnet zero was allowed; on today's exam the zero and all-ones subnets both count.

check.question: Network 10.0.0.0/8 is subnetted with a /16 mask. How many subnets are there, and how many usable hosts in each?
check.explanation: Going from /8 to /16 borrows s = 8 bits, so 2^8 = 256 subnets. That leaves h = 16 host bits, so 2^16 - 2 = 65,534 hosts. 254 subnets uses the outdated minus-2 rule, and 65,536 forgets to subtract the subnet ID and broadcast.

sections.title: The magic number method
sections.body:
On exam day you will see something like: host 192.168.5.77 uses mask 255.255.255.224; which subnet is it in? You need the answer in seconds, not after a page of binary. The **magic number** method (also called the block size method) does it in decimal.

1. Find the **interesting octet**: the one octet where the mask is neither 255 nor 0. For 255.255.255.224 it is the fourth.
2. **Magic number = 256 - mask octet.** 256 - 224 = 32, so subnets start every 32 addresses in that octet.
3. **Subnet ID:** list multiples of the magic number starting at 0 (0, 32, 64, 96, ...) and take the highest one that is not above the address's octet. 77 sits between 64 and 96, so the octet is 64. Octets to the left of the interesting octet are copied, and octets to the right become 0. Subnet ID: 192.168.5.64.
4. **Broadcast:** the next subnet ID minus 1. The next subnet starts at .96, so the broadcast is 192.168.5.95.
5. **Usable hosts:** subnet ID + 1 through broadcast - 1, so 192.168.5.65 to 192.168.5.94. That is 30 hosts, which matches 2^5 - 2.

Run it once more on 10.10.10.200/28. Convert /28 to its mask first: 255.255.255.240. The magic number is 16, the multiples near 200 are 176, 192, 208, so the subnet is 10.10.10.192, the broadcast is 10.10.10.207, and hosts run from .193 to .206.

The method works for every mask. The only things to memorize are the mask octet values (128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254) and the subtraction from 256.
sections.code:
192.168.5.77 /27      mask 255.255.255.224
Interesting octet: 4th (224)     Magic number: 256 - 224 = 32

Multiples of 32:  0   32   64 [77]  96   128   160   192   224
                           ^ highest multiple not above 77

Subnet ID   192.168.5.64     copy 192.168.5, then 64
Broadcast   192.168.5.95     next subnet (96) minus 1
Hosts       192.168.5.65 to 192.168.5.94   (30 usable)
sections.pitfall: Forgetting that the multiples start at 0. With a magic number of 64 the subnets are .0, .64, .128, and .192; starting your count at 64 shifts every answer by one block.

activity.title: Watch the blocks move
activity.prompt: Enter 192.168.5.77 with /27 and confirm the subnet is .64 and the broadcast is .95. Then keep the address and change only the prefix to /26, /28, and /29. Notice the magic number halving each time and the subnet ID snapping to the nearest multiple at or below 77.

check.question: What is the subnet ID for 10.0.0.155/29?
check.explanation: /29 is 255.255.255.248, so the magic number is 8. Multiples of 8 near 155 are 144, 152, 160, and the highest not above 155 is 152. 160 is the next subnet, which makes 10.0.0.159 the broadcast.

sections.title: The binary method, and why the shortcut works
sections.body:
The magic number is a shortcut. Knowing what it is a shortcut for is what saves you when a question is worded in an unusual way or shows you bits.

A device finds its subnet by **ANDing** the address with the mask, bit by bit: a mask bit of 1 keeps the address bit, and a mask bit of 0 forces it to 0. The result is the subnet ID. Setting every host bit to 1 instead gives the broadcast.

Take 172.16.150.77/20. The mask is 255.255.240.0, so the first two octets are copied and the fourth becomes 0 in the subnet ID (255 in the broadcast). Only the third octet needs bit math, shown below. The subnet ID is 172.16.144.0 and the broadcast is 172.16.159.255.

Now check with the magic number: 256 - 240 = 16, and the highest multiple of 16 not above 150 is 144. The next subnet starts at 160, so the broadcast's third octet is 159. Same answer.

Why do the two always agree? The mask octet 11110000 keeps only the 128, 64, 32, and 16 bits of the address octet. Any sum of those place values is a multiple of 16, and 16 is exactly 256 - 240. The bits it clears (8, 4, 2, 1) are the remainder you drop when you round down to a multiple of the block.

Use binary to double-check an answer, when a question shows bits, or while a mask still feels unfamiliar. Use the magic number for speed.
sections.pitfall: Doing bit math on every octet. Only the octet with a partial mask needs it. Octets with mask 255 are copied, and octets with mask 0 become 0 in the subnet ID and 255 in the broadcast.

activity.title: Easy drill: prove both methods agree
activity.prompt: Solve five easy problems. For the first two, write the interesting octet in binary and AND it with the mask before you answer. For the rest, use the magic number, then check that the binary AND would land on the same subnet ID.

check.question: An address's third octet is 01101101 (109) and the mask's third octet is 11111000 (248). What is the subnet ID's third octet?
check.explanation: ANDing keeps the first five bits: 01101000 = 64 + 32 + 8 = 104. The magic number agrees: 256 - 248 = 8, and 104 is the highest multiple of 8 not above 109. 111 is the broadcast's third octet, not the ID's.

sections.title: Any octet: when the interesting octet is not the last
sections.body:
Plenty of exam questions put the interesting octet in the third or second octet, and that is where most mistakes happen. The method is the same; only the bookkeeping changes. Apply this to every octet:

- **Mask 255:** copy the address octet into both the subnet ID and the broadcast.
- **Interesting octet:** the subnet ID gets the multiple of the magic number; the broadcast gets that multiple + magic number - 1.
- **Mask 0:** the subnet ID gets 0; the broadcast gets 255.

**Third octet: 172.20.98.200/21.** The mask is 255.255.248.0 and the magic number is 8. Multiples of 8 near 98: 88, 96, 104. So 98 is in the 96 block. Subnet ID 172.20.96.0. Broadcast: 96 + 8 - 1 = 103 in the third octet and 255 in the fourth, so 172.20.103.255. Hosts run from 172.20.96.1 to 172.20.103.254, which is 2^11 - 2 = 2,046 hosts.

**Second octet: 10.77.200.5/12.** The mask is 255.240.0.0 and the magic number is 16. Multiples near 77: 64, 80. Subnet ID 10.64.0.0. Broadcast 10.79.255.255. Hosts 10.64.0.1 to 10.79.255.254.

Once a subnet spans several values of the third octet, addresses that look reserved may be ordinary hosts. In 10.1.4.0/23 (magic number 2 in the third octet), the range is 10.1.4.0 to 10.1.5.255. So 10.1.4.255 and 10.1.5.0 are perfectly good host addresses, while 10.1.5.255 is the broadcast. Never decide an address is reserved just because its last octet is 0 or 255.
sections.pitfall: Writing the broadcast with only the interesting octet changed, like 172.20.103.0. Every octet to the right of the interesting one is 255 in the broadcast, so the answer is 172.20.103.255.

activity.title: Medium drill: the third octet
activity.prompt: Medium problems move the interesting octet left. Before each answer, say which octet is interesting and what the magic number is. Notice that the broadcast always has 255 in every octet to the right of the interesting one, and the subnet ID always has 0 there.

check.question: What is the subnet ID of 10.200.33.44 with mask 255.255.224.0?
check.explanation: The interesting octet is the third (224), so the magic number is 32. The highest multiple of 32 not above 33 is 32, and the fourth octet becomes 0: 10.200.32.0. 10.200.33.0 treats the mask as a /24.

sections.title: Choosing a mask for a requirement
sections.body:
Your manager hands you 172.16.0.0/16 and says: we need 200 subnets, and the largest must hold 120 hosts, with one mask everywhere. This is the design direction, the reverse of the last three sections. Work out the bits each requirement needs, then see what is left:

1. **Host bits:** the smallest h where 2^h - 2 is at least the host count. For 120 hosts, 2^7 - 2 = 126, so h = 7.
2. **Subnet bits:** the smallest s where 2^s is at least the subnet count. For 200 subnets, 2^8 = 256, so s = 8.
3. **Check the fit:** a /16 leaves 16 bits to split. 8 + 7 = 15, so one bit is spare.
4. **Place the spare bits.** Every prefix from /24 (s = 8, h = 8) to /25 (s = 9, h = 7) meets the requirement. To get the most hosts per subnet, give the spare bits to hosts: /24. To get the most subnets, give them to the subnet field: /25.

For a single LAN only step 1 matters. A LAN with 50 hosts needs h = 6 (62 usable), so a /26. A LAN with exactly 62 hosts still fits a /26. A LAN with 63 does not: it needs h = 7, a /25.

Count every device that needs an address. The router's gateway address, printers, access points, and an HSRP virtual IP all use host addresses. A LAN with 62 PCs plus its router interface needs 63 addresses, so a /26 is one short and the answer is a /25.
sections.code:
Need                     Host bits   Prefix   Usable hosts
2 hosts (router link)    h = 2       /30      2
6 hosts                  h = 3       /29      6
14 hosts                 h = 4       /28      14
30 hosts                 h = 5       /27      30
50 hosts                 h = 6       /26      62
100 hosts                h = 7       /25      126
200 hosts                h = 8       /24      254
500 hosts                h = 9       /23      510
1,000 hosts              h = 10      /22      1,022
sections.pitfall: Comparing the host count with 2^h instead of 2^h - 2. A /26 has 64 addresses but only 62 usable hosts, so it cannot hold 64 hosts, or 62 PCs plus a gateway.

check.question: What is the longest prefix that supports a LAN of 29 hosts plus one router interface?
check.explanation: 29 hosts plus the router is 30 addresses. A /27 has 2^5 - 2 = 30 usable, an exact fit. A /28 gives only 14. /26 also works but is not the longest prefix that fits.

sections.title: VLSM: design from largest to smallest
sections.body:
Real networks are lopsided: a user LAN with 100 hosts, a server LAN with 50, a phone VLAN with 20, and router-to-router links that need just 2 addresses. One mask for everything would either waste huge blocks on the links or be too small for the users. **VLSM** (variable-length subnet masking) lets each subnet use the mask that fits it.

The rule that keeps a VLSM plan clean: **allocate the largest subnets first**, each one starting at the next free address that is a multiple of its own block size. Big blocks land on big boundaries, and small blocks fill the leftover space without overlapping. In the plan below for 192.168.50.0/24, each subnet ID is a valid boundary for its own mask: .128 is a multiple of 64, .192 a multiple of 32, and .224 and .228 multiples of 4. The rest, .232 to .255, stays free for later (a /29 at .232, a /28 at .240, or more /30s).

**Point-to-point links.** A link between two routers needs exactly two addresses. A **/30** (255.255.255.252) has 4 addresses: subnet ID, two hosts, broadcast. That is the classic choice. A **/31** (255.255.255.254, RFC 3021) has just 2 addresses and no subnet ID or broadcast; both are usable, because on a point-to-point link there is nobody else to broadcast to. IOS accepts a /31 on a router-to-router link (on Ethernet it warns you to use it cautiously, but it works). A **/32** is a single address, used for loopback interfaces and host routes.

**Finding overlaps.** A broken VLSM design often shows up as some hosts that cannot reach certain subnets. Calculate each subnet's range, list the subnets in order of subnet ID, and compare each range with the next. In the second table below, 172.16.4.0/23 runs to 172.16.5.255, so it contains 172.16.5.0/24: those two overlap even though their subnet IDs differ.
sections.pitfall: Allocating small subnets first. Put a /30 at .0 and the /25 for 100 hosts can no longer start at .0; it has to move to .128, and the plan quickly runs out of aligned space for the other large subnets.

check.question: In a VLSM plan, the last subnet allocated was 192.168.50.192/27. Where should the next /30 start?
check.explanation: 192.168.50.192/27 ends at its broadcast, .223. The next free address is .224, which is a multiple of 4, so it is a valid /30 boundary. .223 is still inside the /27, and .226 is not a multiple of 4.

sections.title: Summarizing routes
sections.body:
Router R2 connects four LANs: 172.16.0.0/24, 172.16.1.0/24, 172.16.2.0/24, and 172.16.3.0/24. Instead of advertising four routes toward the core, it can advertise one: 172.16.0.0/22. That is **route summarization** (also called aggregation), and it is the other big gift of CIDR: smaller routing tables, and fewer updates rippling through the network when one LAN goes up and down.

To find the smallest summary for a group of contiguous subnets:

1. Find the octet where the subnets differ and write those values in binary.
2. Count how many leading bits all of them share in that octet.
3. The summary prefix is 8 for each octet to the left plus the shared bits. The summary address keeps the shared bits and sets everything after them to 0.

For 10.1.8.0/24 through 10.1.15.0/24, the third octet runs from 8 (00001000) to 15 (00001111). The first 5 bits (00001) match, so the prefix is 16 + 5 = /21 and the summary is 10.1.8.0/21. Check with the magic number: a /21 has a block of 8 in the third octet, and 8 is a multiple of 8, so 10.1.8.0/21 is a real boundary covering 10.1.8.0 to 10.1.15.255.

A summary must start on a boundary of its own size, which is why some groups cannot be summarized exactly. 192.168.4.0/24 through 192.168.6.0/24 cannot be summarized as 192.168.4.0/23 (that covers only 4 and 5). The smallest single summary is 192.168.4.0/22, which also includes 192.168.7.0/24. A summary that covers addresses you did not intend is an **inexact summary**. It is harmless if 192.168.7.0/24 is unused, but if that subnet lives somewhere else in the network, the summary can attract traffic for it to the wrong router.
sections.code:
Summarize 10.1.8.0/24 through 10.1.15.0/24

Third octet    8 = 00001 000
               9 = 00001 001
              ...
              15 = 00001 111
                   ^^^^^ 5 shared bits

Prefix:  8 + 8 (first two octets) + 5 = /21
Summary: 10.1.8.0/21   covers 10.1.8.0 to 10.1.15.255
sections.pitfall: Choosing a summary address that is not on its own boundary, such as 192.168.4.0/21. A /21 has a block of 8 in the third octet, so its networks start at 0, 8, 16, and so on. The /21 containing 192.168.4.0 is 192.168.0.0/21.

check.question: What is the smallest single summary for 172.16.32.0/24, 172.16.33.0/24, 172.16.34.0/24, and 172.16.35.0/24?
check.explanation: 32 to 35 in binary are 00100000 to 00100011: the first 6 bits match, so 16 + 6 = /22. 172.16.32.0/22 covers exactly 32.0 to 35.255. A /23 covers only 32 and 33, and a /21 would add 36 to 39.

sections.title: Traps and exam speed
sections.body:
Most wrong subnetting answers do not come from misunderstanding. They come from a handful of repeat mistakes. Learn to catch them in your own work:

- **Subnet zero.** Count 2^s subnets, not 2^s - 2. The zero subnet (same number as the original network, such as 172.16.0.0/24 inside 172.16.0.0/16) and the all-ones subnet are both usable.
- **Off-by-one hosts.** A subnet has 2^h addresses but 2^h - 2 hosts, and the router's gateway address is one of those hosts.
- **Wrong octet.** /21 makes the third octet interesting, not the fourth. Someone who answers 10.1.70.0 for 10.1.70.5/21 treated it as a /24. The right answer is 10.1.64.0.
- **Forgetting the octets to the right.** They are 0 in the subnet ID and 255 in the broadcast.
- **Judging by the last octet.** 10.10.15.255/21 is a broadcast address (the subnet runs 10.10.8.0 to 10.10.15.255), while 10.10.14.255/21 is an ordinary host.
- **Gateway in another subnet.** A host at 10.1.1.70/26 lives in 10.1.1.64/26 (.64 to .127). If its gateway is set to 10.1.1.62, that gateway is in 10.1.1.0/26, so the host can reach local neighbors but nothing beyond them.

For speed, memorize the table below, then practice until a fourth-octet problem takes under 15 seconds and a third-octet problem under 30. Write the multiples of the magic number on your scratch board rather than juggling them in your head. The goal on exam day is to spend your minutes on the long scenario questions, not on arithmetic.
sections.pitfall: Starting the arithmetic before identifying the interesting octet. Write the mask in dotted decimal first and circle the octet that is neither 255 nor 0; everything else follows from that.

activity.title: Hard drill against the clock
activity.prompt: Hard problems mix all octets and larger prefixes. Time yourself and aim for under 30 seconds each. When you miss one, name the trap from this section that caused it before moving on.

check.question: Which of these addresses is a subnet broadcast address?
check.explanation: A /19 has a magic number of 32 in the third octet, so 172.16.31.255 is in 172.16.0.0/19, whose broadcast is 172.16.31.255. 172.16.32.255 is a host in 172.16.32.0/19, 10.0.0.255/23 is a host in 10.0.0.0/23, and 192.168.1.128/25 is a subnet ID.

keyTerms.definition: Host bits borrowed to number subnets; s borrowed bits create 2^s subnets.
The bits left after the prefix; h host bits give 2^h - 2 usable hosts per subnet.
The one octet where the mask is neither 255 nor 0; all the subnet math happens there.
256 minus the mask value in the interesting octet; subnet IDs are multiples of it. Also called the block size.
The first address of a subnet, with all host bits 0; also called the subnet number or network address.
The first subnet of a network, with the same number as the network itself; usable by default in IOS and on the exam.
Variable-length subnet masking: using different masks for different subnets of one network, allocated largest first.
Point-to-point link sizes: a /30 has 2 usable hosts plus ID and broadcast; a /31 has 2 addresses, both usable.
Advertising one shorter prefix that covers several contiguous subnets, such as 172.16.0.0/22 for four /24s.
A summary that also covers addresses outside the subnets being summarized.
How a device finds the subnet ID: mask bits of 1 keep address bits, mask bits of 0 clear them.

summary: Subnets = 2^s (zero and all-ones subnets count); usable hosts = 2^h - 2.
Magic number = 256 - mask in the interesting octet; the subnet ID is the highest multiple not above the address, and the broadcast is the next subnet minus 1.
Octets left of the interesting one are copied; octets right of it are 0 in the subnet ID and 255 in the broadcast.
To pick a mask, find the host bits and subnet bits needed, check they fit, and place spare bits by what the question wants to maximize.
VLSM allocates the largest subnets first on their own boundaries; use /30 or /31 for router links and check ranges for overlaps.
Summarize contiguous subnets by counting shared leading bits, and make sure the summary starts on its own boundary.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Teach a classmate how to find the subnet ID, broadcast address, and usable range of 172.20.98.200/21 with the magic number, show why a router gets the same answer by ANDing in binary, and explain why a VLSM plan allocates the biggest subnets first.

questions.question: When you subnet a network, which bits do you borrow to create the subnet field?
choices: Bits from the original network part
Bits from the first octet of the mask
questions.explanation: Subnetting turns some host bits into subnet bits, making the prefix longer. The original network bits never change; that is why every subnet still starts with the same network number.

questions.question: How many usable host addresses are in a /27 subnet?
questions.explanation: /27 leaves 5 host bits: 2^5 = 32 addresses, minus the subnet ID and broadcast, gives 30.

questions.question: Network 172.16.0.0/16 is subnetted using a /22 mask. How many subnets does that create?
questions.explanation: From /16 to /22 borrows 6 bits, and 2^6 = 64. Each /22 has 10 host bits, or 1,022 usable hosts.

questions.question: Network 10.0.0.0/8 is subnetted with mask 255.255.240.0. How many subnets result?
questions.explanation: 255.255.240.0 is /20. From /8 to /20 borrows 12 bits: 2^12 = 4,096 subnets, each with 2^12 - 2 = 4,094 hosts.

questions.question: Unless a CCNA question says otherwise, how should you treat the zero subnet and the last (all-ones) subnet?
choices: Neither is usable, so s subnet bits give 2^s - 2 subnets
Only the zero subnet is usable, giving 2^s - 1 subnets
Both are usable, so s subnet bits give 2^s subnets
They are usable only when VLSM is in use
questions.explanation: IOS allows the zero subnet by default (ip subnet-zero), and the exam assumes both special subnets are usable. The 2^s - 2 rule is a leftover from older practice. Hosts still use 2^h - 2.

questions.question: Match each prefix length to its number of usable hosts.
questions.explanation: Host bits are 32 minus the prefix, and usable hosts are 2^h - 2: /30 has 2 host bits (2), /29 has 3 (6), /28 has 4 (14), /27 has 5 (30), /26 has 6 (62).

questions.question: A /24 network is split into /26 subnets. Which list shows the subnet IDs' fourth octets?
questions.explanation: /26 is mask 255.255.255.192, so the magic number is 256 - 192 = 64 and subnets start at multiples of 64. 1, 65, 129, 193 are the first hosts, not the subnet IDs.

questions.question: What is the magic number (block size) for the mask 255.255.255.240?
questions.explanation: 256 - 240 = 16, so subnets start at .0, .16, .32, and so on.

questions.question: What is the subnet ID of 192.168.5.77/27?
questions.explanation: /27 is 255.255.255.224, magic number 32. The highest multiple of 32 not above 77 is 64.

questions.question: What is the broadcast address of the subnet containing 192.168.5.77/27?
questions.explanation: The subnet is 192.168.5.64 and the next one starts at 192.168.5.96, so the broadcast is one less: 192.168.5.95.

questions.question: What is the first usable host address in the subnet containing 10.10.10.200/28?
questions.explanation: /28 has a magic number of 16. The highest multiple of 16 not above 200 is 192, so the subnet is 10.10.10.192 and the first host is .193. The broadcast is .207.

questions.question: What is the last usable host address in the subnet containing 172.16.1.100/26?
questions.explanation: /26 has a magic number of 64. 100 falls in the 64 block, so the subnet is 172.16.1.64, the broadcast is 172.16.1.127, and the last host is 172.16.1.126.

questions.question: Put the steps of the magic number method in order.
items: Identify the interesting octet, where the mask is neither 255 nor 0
Subtract that mask octet from 256 to get the magic number
Pick the highest multiple of the magic number not above the address octet
Write the subnet ID: copied octets, that multiple, then zeros
Add the magic number to find the next subnet ID, then subtract 1 for the broadcast
Take subnet ID + 1 and broadcast - 1 as the usable range
questions.explanation: Everything keys off the interesting octet, so find it first. The broadcast depends on the next subnet ID, and the host range depends on both the subnet ID and the broadcast.

questions.question: Using binary if you like, find the subnet ID of 10.33.181.9/20.
questions.explanation: 181 is 10110101. ANDing with 240 (11110000) keeps 10110000 = 176. Magic number check: 256 - 240 = 16, and the highest multiple of 16 not above 181 is 176.

questions.question: An address's third octet is 10010110 and the mask's third octet is 11110000. What is the third octet of the subnet ID in decimal?
questions.explanation: The AND keeps the first four bits and clears the rest: 10010000 = 128 + 16 = 144. 150 is the original address octet and 159 is the broadcast's third octet.

questions.question: What is the broadcast address of the subnet containing 10.33.181.9/20?
questions.explanation: The subnet is 10.33.176.0. The magic number is 16, so the next subnet is 10.33.192.0 and the broadcast is 10.33.191.255. In binary, the host bits of the third octet become 1: 10111111 = 191.

questions.question: Why does ANDing an address with mask 255.255.255.224 always give a fourth octet that is a multiple of 32?
questions.answer: 224 is 11100000, so the AND keeps only the 128, 64, and 32 bits of the address octet and clears the 16, 8, 4, 2, and 1 bits. Any sum of 128, 64, and 32 is a multiple of 32, which is the magic number 256 - 224.
questions.explanation: This is why the magic number shortcut and the binary method always agree: rounding down to a multiple of the block size is the same as clearing the host bits.

questions.question: What is the subnet ID of 172.20.98.200/21?
questions.explanation: /21 is 255.255.248.0, so the third octet is interesting with a magic number of 8. 98 falls in the 96 block, and the fourth octet becomes 0.

questions.question: What is the broadcast address of the subnet containing 172.20.98.200/21?
questions.explanation: The subnet is 172.20.96.0 and the next one is 172.20.104.0, so the broadcast is 172.20.103.255. The fourth octet is 255 because it is to the right of the interesting octet.

questions.question: What is the subnet ID of 10.77.200.5/12?
questions.explanation: /12 is 255.240.0.0, so the second octet is interesting with a magic number of 16. 77 falls in the 64 block, and the third and fourth octets become 0. The subnet runs to 10.79.255.255.

questions.question: Which of these are usable host addresses in the subnet 10.1.4.0/23? Choose three.
questions.explanation: 10.1.4.0/23 spans 10.1.4.0 to 10.1.5.255. Only the first (subnet ID) and last (broadcast) are reserved, so 10.1.4.255 and 10.1.5.0 are ordinary hosts. 10.1.6.1 belongs to the next subnet, 10.1.6.0/23.

questions.question: For the address 10.50.70.90 with mask 255.255.192.0, which octet is interesting and what is the magic number?
questions.explanation: The third mask octet (192) is the one that is neither 255 nor 0, and 256 - 192 = 64. So the subnet is 10.50.64.0 and the broadcast is 10.50.127.255.

questions.question: What is the longest prefix length (smallest subnet) that supports 50 hosts?
questions.explanation: You need 2^h - 2 of at least 50. h = 5 gives only 30, while h = 6 gives 62. Six host bits means a /26.

questions.question: A LAN has 62 PCs and also needs an address for its router interface. What is the longest prefix length that fits?
questions.explanation: 62 PCs plus the gateway is 63 addresses. A /26 has 62 usable hosts, one short, so you need 7 host bits: a /25 with 126 hosts.

questions.question: Network 172.16.0.0/16 must support 200 subnets, each with up to 120 hosts, using one mask throughout. Which mask meets the requirements and gives the most hosts per subnet?
questions.explanation: 200 subnets need s = 8 (256) and 120 hosts need h = 7 (126). From /16 that is 15 of the 16 bits, so /24 and /25 both work; /24 gives more hosts (254). /23 gives only 128 subnets and /26 only 62 hosts.

questions.question: Network 10.0.0.0/8 needs at least 1,000 subnets with up to 2,000 hosts each, one mask throughout. Which masks meet the requirements? Choose three.
questions.explanation: 1,000 subnets need s = 10 (1,024), so the prefix must be at least /18. 2,000 hosts need h = 11 (2,046), so the prefix can be at most /21. /18, /19, and /21 all fit. /22 leaves 1,022 hosts and /17 gives only 512 subnets.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of subnet bits needed to create at least 50 subnets?
questions.explanation: 2^5 = 32 is too few and 2^6 = 64 is enough, so 6 subnet bits.

questions.question: You are building a VLSM plan from 192.168.50.0/24. Put these subnets in the order you should allocate them.
questions.explanation: Allocate largest first so each block starts on its own boundary and the small ones fill the gaps. Starting small fragments the space.

questions.question: From 192.168.50.0/24, Users (100 hosts) received 192.168.50.0/25. Servers need 50 hosts. What subnet, with prefix, do they get next?
questions.explanation: 50 hosts need a /26 (62 hosts). The next free address after the /25 is .128, which is a multiple of 64, so Servers get 192.168.50.128/26 (.129 to .190).

questions.question: Continuing the plan: after 192.168.50.128/26, Phones need 20 hosts. What subnet, with prefix, do they get?
questions.explanation: 20 hosts need a /27 (30 hosts). The /26 ends at .191, so the next free address is .192, a multiple of 32. Phones get .193 to .222.

questions.question: Some hosts in this VLSM design cannot reach each other. Which two subnets overlap?
questions.explanation: 172.16.4.0/23 runs from 172.16.4.0 to 172.16.5.255, which contains all of 172.16.5.0/24. R1's /23 ends at 172.16.3.255, and the two /30s are 9.0 to 9.3 and 9.4 to 9.7, so those do not overlap.

questions.question: What does a /31 mask give a point-to-point link between two routers?
choices: One usable address plus a broadcast
Two addresses, both usable, with no subnet ID or broadcast
questions.explanation: RFC 3021 lets a /31 use both of its addresses on a point-to-point link, since there are only two devices and no need for a broadcast. A /30 is the four-address option with two usable hosts.

questions.question: R1's G0/1 connects to R2 over the link 10.0.0.8/30. Type the interface command that gives R1 the first usable address in that subnet.
questions.explanation: 10.0.0.8/30 contains .8 (subnet ID), .9 and .10 (hosts), and .11 (broadcast). R1 takes .9 with mask 255.255.255.252, and R2 would take .10.

questions.question: What single route summarizes 172.16.0.0/24, 172.16.1.0/24, 172.16.2.0/24, and 172.16.3.0/24 exactly?
questions.explanation: Third octets 0 to 3 are 000000xx: 6 shared bits, so 16 + 6 = /22. 172.16.0.0/22 covers 172.16.0.0 to 172.16.3.255 and nothing else.

questions.question: What is the smallest single summary route for 10.1.8.0/24 through 10.1.15.0/24?
questions.explanation: 8 to 15 in binary are 00001000 to 00001111: 5 shared bits, so 16 + 5 = /21. 8 is a multiple of the /21 block size (8), so 10.1.8.0/21 is a valid boundary covering exactly those eight /24s.

questions.question: What is the smallest single summary that includes 192.168.4.0/24, 192.168.5.0/24, and 192.168.6.0/24?
questions.explanation: 4, 5, and 6 share the leading bits 000001, so /22 is the longest prefix that covers all three; 192.168.4.0/22 also includes 192.168.7.0, making it inexact. A /23 at .4 misses 6, and 192.168.4.0/21 is not a valid boundary (a /21 starts at multiples of 8).

questions.question: Which of these routes fall inside the summary 10.20.16.0/20? Choose two.
questions.explanation: A /20 has a block of 16 in the third octet, so 10.20.16.0/20 spans 10.20.16.0 to 10.20.31.255. 10.20.32.0 is the next block, and 15.0 and 0.0 belong to 10.20.0.0/20.

questions.question: A PC is configured as shown. It can reach hosts on its own LAN but nothing beyond it. What is wrong?
questions.code:
IPv4 Address . . . . . : 10.1.1.70
Subnet Mask  . . . . . : 255.255.255.192
Default Gateway  . . . : 10.1.1.62
choices: The gateway is in a different subnet than the PC
The gateway must be the last usable address
questions.explanation: With /26, the PC is in 10.1.1.64/26 (.64 to .127), but 10.1.1.62 is in 10.1.1.0/26. The PC cannot ARP for a gateway outside its own subnet. Either the gateway or the PC's address and mask is wrong.

questions.question: Which of these addresses cannot be assigned to a host?
questions.explanation: A /21 has a magic number of 8 in the third octet, so 10.10.15.255 sits in 10.10.8.0/21 (8.0 to 15.255) and is its broadcast. 10.10.14.255 and 10.10.12.0 are ordinary hosts inside that range, and 192.168.10.65 is the first host of 192.168.10.64/26.

questions.question: A student says the subnet ID of 10.1.70.5/21 is 10.1.70.0. What went wrong, and what is the right answer?
choices: They forgot to subtract 2; the subnet is 10.1.68.0
They worked as if it were a /24; the third octet is interesting, so the subnet is 10.1.64.0
They skipped subnet zero; the subnet is 10.1.72.0
questions.explanation: /21 is 255.255.248.0, so the third octet is interesting with a magic number of 8. The highest multiple of 8 not above 70 is 64, giving 10.1.64.0 (range 10.1.64.0 to 10.1.71.255).
